# “I Didn't Have to Struggle”: Caregivers’ Perspectives on the Synergistic Interplay of WIC and SNAP on Family Health

**Authors:** Cristina M. Gago; Matthew M. Lee; Nour M. Hammad; Jhordan O. Wynne; Mary Kathryn Poole; Meghan Zimmer; Rebecca S. Mozaffarian; Rachel Colchamiro; Kelley May; Eric B. Rimm; Erica L. Kenney

**Affiliations:** Cristina M. Gago is with the Department of Community Health Sciences, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA. Matthew M. Lee is with the Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston. Nour M. Hammad, Jhordan O. Wynne, Mary Kathryn Poole, Meghan Zimmer, and Rebecca S. Mozaffarian are with the Department of Nutrition, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health. Rachel Colchamiro and Kelley May are with the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, Boston. Eric B. Rimm is with the Department of Nutrition and the Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, and the Channing Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston. Erica L. Kenney is with the Department of Nutrition and the Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health.

## Abstract

We explored how increased Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits interacted for dually enrolled households. Twenty-five parents dually enrolled in WIC and SNAP in the spring of 2020 shared perceptions of expanded benefits and reduced administrative requirements via semistructured interviews. Specifically, parents shared that benefit increases minimized monthly cycles of limited or uncertain access to food, barriers to WIC redemption led many to prioritize SNAP benefits, reduced administrative requirements facilitated staying enrolled in both programs, and administrative flexibilities and benefit increases supported WIC and SNAP utilization.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, when millions reported not having enough to eat and social distancing hindered access to services, Congress allowed the US Department of Agriculture to temporarily decrease administrative requirements and increase benefits for the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP; Appendix B Table A, available as a supplement to the online version of this article at https://ajph.org). Changes to WIC allowed parents to recertify remotely and increased the cash value benefit for fruit and vegetable purchases from $9 to, currently, $26 per month per child. Simultaneously, SNAP extended the time between households’ recertification applications, waived application interviews, permitted online shopping, and increased benefits (Appendix B, Figure A).

While growing literature has examined the impact of these changes on households enrolled in either WIC1-4 or SNAP5-7 alone,8 few have examined the interplay across programs, despite one in three WIC-enrolled families participating in SNAP concurrently.9 Better understanding of household experiences using both programs is critical for improving utilization.

## STUDY OBJECTIVE

This qualitative study aimed to improve understanding of how expanded benefits and reduced administrative burden in WIC and SNAP simultaneously influenced eligible households’ retention and utilization decisions.

## RESEARCH QUESTION

How did expanded benefits and reduced administrative burden in WIC and SNAP influence dually eligible households’ participation and utilization decisions?

## PARTICIPANTS, SAMPLE, LOCATION, SETTING, AND YEAR OF STUDY

Parents with children who self-reported being enrolled in both WIC and SNAP in March 2020, were at least 18 years old, lived in Massachusetts, and spoke English or Spanish were eligible (December 2023–March 2024). All participants (n = 25) identified as female (Table A). Most were aged older than 30 years (54.2%), spoke English at home (62.5%), and identified as Puerto Rican (62.5%). Half reported sometimes worrying food would run out in the past year.

## METHODS

This qualitative study was conducted in partnership with Massachusetts WIC.

### Recruitment and Data Collection

Local WIC programs and community organizations shared information about the study via e-mail and text messages, social media, and physical flyer distribution. Interested participants contacted the study team via phone, e-mail, or QR code to complete an online eligibility screener. Researchers followed up with those deemed eligible to schedule an interview. After providing written informed consent, participants completed a brief demographic survey and a 45-minute semistructured Zoom interview. Interviews were led by trained qualitative researchers and audio recorded. Reporting aligns with the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research.

### Conceptual Framework and Interview Design

Our interview guide and analytic approach were grounded in the Getting to Equity Framework.10 The framework posits four interrelated constructs as drivers of nutritional inequities, including increasing access to healthy food, reducing deterrents, improving resources, and building capacity. The study team developed a semistructured interview guide exploring these four constructs in relation to WIC and SNAP participation experiences, pandemic-related program changes, and the interaction between WIC and SNAP administrative burdens and benefits (Appendix A, available as a supplement to the online version of this article at https://www.ajph.org). We piloted the guide with two WIC participants and subsequently revised.

### Analysis

Audio was transcribed verbatim by Sonix software (San Francisco, CA) and transcripts were analyzed by four trained researchers (C. M. G., M. M. L., N. M. H., and J. O. W.; see Appendix B, available as a supplement to the online version of this article at https://ajph.org, for positionality) in Dedoose 9.0.17 (Sociocultural Research Consultants LLC, Los Angeles, CA).11 C. M. G. developed a preliminary codebook based on the Getting to Equity Framework,10 predefined topics from the interview guide, and emergent topics from transcript review. Via deductive thematic analysis,12 the researchers applied codes to the same five transcripts—meeting to iteratively revise the codebook, review code applications, and discuss discrepancies until reaching consensus. Once coding was deemed consistent, a team of analysts (C. M. G., M. M. L., N. M. H., and J. O. W.) coded the remaining transcripts independently. Researchers then reviewed the coded excerpts and met to generate, refine, and finalize themes through discussion.

## KEY FINDINGS

Two key findings were identified. First, expanded WIC and SNAP benefits promoted dual program utilization; however, pandemic circumstances forced greater reliance on SNAP. Second, reduced administrative requirements for WIC and SNAP supported dual program retention, but differences in the quality of interactions with WIC and SNAP staff impacted participants’ experiences of these changes.

### Expanded Benefits Promoted Utilization

#### Increases to WIC and SNAP benefits served distinct, though synergistic, missions.

Participants viewed the purposes of WIC and SNAP to be distinct. For example, they reported that WIC’s cash value benefit increase aligned with WIC’s goal to promote nutrition—allowing them to buy greater quantity, quality, and variety of fruits and vegetables (Box 1). Meanwhile, participants reported that SNAP’s temporary emergency allotments and permanent Thrifty Food Plan adjustment improved access to flexible economic resources for poverty alleviation. Benefit increases interacted to facilitate benefit redemption across programs; for example, parents reported that increases in WIC’s cash value benefit allowed them to save and stretch SNAP dollars further. However, the end of SNAP emergency allotments brought a return to monthly cycles of limited or uncertain food access.

#### Pandemic supply chain issues and fear of illness hindered access to WIC-approved foods, forcing greater reliance on SNAP.

Parents identified three hindrances to WIC benefit uptake at the pandemic’s start: low in-store inventory, transit barriers, and inability to shop in store for fear of COVID-19 exposure. Low inventory meant parents often could not fully redeem WIC benefits, even after traveling to multiple stores. Fear of illness led many to avoid stores, even if it meant forfeiting WIC benefits. Alternatively, SNAP benefit increases and flexibilities gave families the resources to stock up on staples through a single monthly trip.

#### Amid SNAP benefit increases, some WIC participants redeemed WIC benefits more selectively.

While grocery access changes drove initial reductions in WIC redemption, most parents still needed and intended to use WIC benefits fully—citing rising food prices and continued monthly cycles of limited or uncertain access to adequate food. However, some parents did note that SNAP benefit increases resulted in their redeeming WIC benefits less, even after initial grocery stocking issues were resolved, especially after the introduction of SNAP online shopping in Massachusetts in June 2020. Leveraging SNAP’s flexibility and convenience, some reported using SNAP dollars on WIC items (and forfeiting WIC benefits) to save additional trips to WIC-approved stores. However, even those who reported under-redeeming components of their WIC food package still fully redeemed WIC’s cash value benefit.

### Reduced Requirements Supported Retention

WIC’s transition to remote appointments was consistently described as the most important administrative change across both programs, ultimately facilitating retention in WIC (Box 2). This was especially true among parents with difficulty traveling to in-person appointments. While most parents reported no change in the quality of services, some felt in-person appointments were more thorough for monitoring growth; these parents advocated hybrid service options. Regarding SNAP, some parents reported that their recertification experiences did not change despite the administrative policy waivers, though some families noted that the extended certification periods protected against financial shocks.

Participants described broken communication with SNAP agency staff, including dropped calls and long wait times when attempting to reach caseworkers. Such interactions perpetuated feelings of shame and stigma. In contrast, open communication and positive relationships offered by WIC facilitated redemption and retention.

## EVALUATION, TRANSFERABILITY, AND ADVERSE EFFECTS

In this study of the interactions between WIC and SNAP among dually enrolled households, parents reported that WIC and SNAP play distinct, though complementary, roles in enhancing food access.8 WIC supports nutritional health and SNAP supports poverty alleviation. Despite intending to use both WIC and SNAP benefits fully, parents faced barriers to WIC access,13 which prompted many to use SNAP’s more flexible benefits to buy WIC items or alternatives. WIC’s cash value benefit, which most closely resembles SNAP benefits in terms of maximizing autonomy, was the most highly valued and redeemed component of WIC’s food package.1-3

Participation in WIC and SNAP for economically disadvantaged households is critical for reducing food insecurity, related health risks, and health care costs. It is also essential for preventing the widening of health inequities, given the intersection of food security with low income and structural racism. Our findings suggest that the pandemic-era streamlining of WIC and SNAP and increased benefit amounts should continue and be expanded—for example, through introducing WIC–SNAP dual-approved online shopping, adding more WIC food package flexibilities, and maintaining remote benefit services. Participants’ description of the critical role of respectful, open communication with WIC agency staff also highlights the need to design policies to support this.

However, most pandemic-era relief programs have ended, resulting in significant increases in food insecurity nationwide (affecting 10.2% in 2021, 12.8% in 2022, and 13.5% in 202314), aligning with the United States’ largest one-year increase in poverty (doubling from 5.2% in 2021 to 12.4% in 2022).15 Despite this, Congress passed legislation to restrict access to SNAP, increase administrative burdens, and reduce benefit amounts over time.16

Study transferability may be limited; most data were collected from participants recruited from one local WIC program in Massachusetts. However, findings align with those from other states5,7 and federal policies examined hold implications for states across the nation.
